title: Streetlight retrofits by ward

blocks.text: A city's public-works department is choosing which streetlight blocks to retrofit with LED fixtures this year. The model in `retrofits.py` already has a binary `x[rid]` per candidate retrofit (1 if it is funded) and a budget row. Two rules from the operations office are missing:

items: **Yards.** The crews of each ward work out of one yard, and a yard can stage at most `yard_cap[ward]` retrofits. A ward that does not appear in `yard_cap` has no yard limit.
**Fair share.** No ward may receive more than `max_share` (a fraction such as 0.4) of the retrofits the plan funds.

blocks.text: Write `add_ward_rules(model, x, retrofits, yard_cap, max_share)` so that the model allows exactly the plans that keep both rules.
The model so far, with $`R`$ the candidate retrofits, $`c_r`$ the cost of retrofit $`r`$ and $`B`$ the budget:

Name the sets and parameters you need (the wards, the retrofits of each ward, the caps, the share), write your rows in this notation first, each with its quantifier and a label, then code them. A share of a count is not linear as a fraction; find the form that is.
The tests fix a plan through the variables' bounds and ask the solver whether the model accepts it, so any correct formulation passes. About six lines.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Retrofit:
    rid: str
    ward: str
    cost: int        # $k


def add_ward_rules(model: mathopt.Model, x: dict, retrofits: list[Retrofit],
                   yard_cap: dict[str, int], max_share: float) -> None:
    """Each ward's yard stages at most yard_cap[ward] retrofits; no ward takes more than max_share of the plan."""
    funded = sum(x.values())
    for ward in sorted({r.ward for r in retrofits}):
        in_ward = sum(x[r.rid] for r in retrofits if r.ward == ward)
        if ward in yard_cap:
            model.add_linear_constraint(in_ward <= yard_cap[ward], name=f"yard_{ward}")
        model.add_linear_constraint(in_ward <= max_share * funded, name=f"share_{ward}")


def build(retrofits: list[Retrofit], budget: int, yard_cap: dict[str, int],
          max_share: float) -> tuple[mathopt.Model, dict]:
    model = mathopt.Model(name="streetlights")
    x = {r.rid: model.add_binary_variable(name=f"x_{r.rid}") for r in retrofits}
    model.add_linear_constraint(sum(r.cost * x[r.rid] for r in retrofits) <= budget, name="budget")
    add_ward_rules(model, x, retrofits, yard_cap, max_share)
    model.maximize(sum(x.values()))
    return model, x


if __name__ == "__main__":
    blocks = [Retrofit("N1", "North", 40), Retrofit("N2", "North", 35), Retrofit("S1", "South", 50)]
    model, x = build(blocks, 200, {"North": 1}, 0.5)
    print(len(list(model.linear_constraints())), "rows")

# Streetlight blocks in four wards: id, ward, cost.
blocks = ([Retrofit(f"A{k}", "Alder", 20 + k) for k in range(1, 5)]
          + [Retrofit(f"B{k}", "Birch", 30 + k) for k in range(1, 4)]
          + [Retrofit(f"C{k}", "Cedar", 15 + k) for k in range(1, 4)])
yards = {"Alder": 3, "Birch": 2}   # Cedar is not listed

    model, x = build(blocks, 5_000, yards, share)

    params = mathopt.SolveParameters(time_limit=timedelta(seconds=5))
    result = mathopt.solve(model, mathopt.SolverType.HIGHS, params=params)
    return result.termination.reason == mathopt.TerminationReason.OPTIMAL

cases.says: a plan within every ward's yard cap is allowed, and one that sends a ward more retrofits than its yard handles is refused
a plan in which one ward takes more than its share of the funded retrofits is refused
a small plan dominated by one ward is refused, although that ward's count is small next to the candidate list
a ward missing from the yard caps has no yard limit, and still may not take more than its share

origin.section: A Counting Row Caps How Many Projects of One Kind Are Funded

concepts: a cap on how many of a kind, and a share of the plan multiplied out, are rows on counts
a sum of binaries over a set counts the funded members, and a weighted sum totals a quantity over them
